hooks.text: You do not need 25,000 miles per hour to escape Earth.
Any speed will work to leave Earth if you keep thrusting.
Escape velocity is not a speed limit you must break.

title: The Escape Velocity Myth
description: Discover why the famous 25,000 miles per hour speed limit is only true if you stop your engines.

beats.text: You do not need 25,000 miles per hour to escape Earth.
beats.visual: Apollo 17 photograph of Earth from space, 1972

beats.text: That massive speed is only required if you use a single unpowered launch boost.
beats.visual: diagram of escape velocity trajectories from a planet

beats.text: If you fire a projectile and let gravity do all the work, you genuinely need 11.2 kilometers per second.
beats.visual: Saturn V rocket liftoff during Apollo mission, 1969

beats.text: But modern rockets are not unpowered cannonballs designed for a single blast.
beats.visual: Space Shuttle liftoff from Kennedy Space Center, 1981

beats.text: By keeping their engines burning, they can climb at a leisurely walking pace and still slip away completely.
beats.visual: International Space Station solar arrays with orbital sunrise, 2011

beats.text: Escape velocity is simply the total energy cost needed to leave Earth for good.
beats.visual: artist concept of a gravity well as a warped grid

beats.text: Thanks to continuous thrust, you do not have to pay that steep gravity bill all at once.
beats.visual: Voyager spacecraft artist concept in deep space, 1977

beats.text: This is why you do not need 25,000 miles per hour to escape Earth.
beats.visual: Apollo 17 photograph of Earth from space, 1972
